author: Seneca
title: For life and health
pd: Ask the gods for life and health; if thou art resolved to die, death’s reward is to have done with prayers.
source: Seneca, *Letters* 117.24. Latin text; Gummere’s translation.
original: Deos vitam et salutem roga; si mori placuit, hic mortis est fructus, optare desinere.
accurate: Ask the gods for life and health. If you have decided to die, this is death’s benefit: to stop wishing.

editions.name: Thomas Lodge
editions.text: Beseech the gods to give thee life and health: if thou hast a mind to die, this is the fruit of death, to give over wishing.

editions.name: Thomas Morell
editions.text: Ask of the Gods, if you please, life, and health: but if you had rather die, the fruit or effect of death is to refrain from wishing.

editions.name: Richard M. Gummere
editions.text: Ask the gods for life and health; if thou art resolved to die, death’s reward is to have done with prayers.

audit: All three complete English Moral Letters translations in scope are represented: Lodge, Morell, and Gummere.

author: Athenians
title: Athenian prayer for rain
pd: A prayer of the Athenians: Rain, rain, O dear Zeus, down on the ploughed fields of the Athenians and on the plains.—In truth we ought not to pray at all, or we ought to pray in this simple and noble fashion.
source: Quoted in Marcus Aurelius, *Meditations* 5.7. Greek text; Long’s translation.
original: Εὐχὴ Ἀθηναίων· ὗσον, ὗσον, ὦ φίλε Ζεῦ, κατὰ τῆς ἀρούρας τῆς Ἀθηναίων καὶ τῶν πεδίων. ἤτοι οὐ δεῖ εὔχεσθαι ἢ οὕτως ἁπλῶς καὶ ἐλευθέρως.
accurate: Prayer of the Athenians: “Rain, rain, dear Zeus, on the Athenians’ plowed land and on their plains.” Either one should not pray, or one should pray so simply and freely.

editions.name: Meric Casaubon
editions.text: The form of the Athenians’ prayer did run thus: ‘O rain, rain, good Jupiter, upon all the grounds and fields that belong to the Athenians.’ Either we should not pray at all, or thus absolutely and freely; and not every one for himself in particular alone.

editions.name: Jeremy Collier
editions.text: A prayer of the Athenians, ‘Send down, oh! send down rain, dear Zeus, on the ploughed fields and plains of the Athenians.’ Of a truth, we should not pray at all, or else in this simple and noble fashion.

editions.name: James Thomson
editions.text: It is an Athenian Form of Prayer. Rain dear Jupiter, Rain on the fields of the Athenians, and on their Meadows. And truly we ought always to pray with the same Freedom and Simplicity, or not to pray at all.

editions.name: Francis Hutcheson and James Moor
editions.text: This is a prayer of the Athenians: “Rain, rain, kind Jupiter! upon the tilled grounds and pastures of the Athenians.” We should either not pray at all, or pray with such simplicity, and such kind affections of free citizens toward our fellows.

editions.name: Richard Graves
editions.text: It was the usual form of supplication, among the Athenians, “O! Jupiter, send us, we beseech thee, send us rain upon all the land, whether tillage or pasture, of the Athenians in general.” We ought to pray in this simple and public-spirited manner, or not to pray at all.

editions.name: Henry McCormac
editions.text: Pray in a more open and generous spirit than was the wont of the Athenians, when they entreated the Almighty to pour fertilizing showers on their fields and lands.

editions.name: George Long
editions.text: A prayer of the Athenians: Rain, rain, O dear Zeus, down on the ploughed fields of the Athenians and on the plains.—In truth we ought not to pray at all, or we ought to pray in this simple and noble fashion.

editions.name: G. H. Rendall
editions.text: An Athenian prayer—Rain, rain, dear Zeus, upon Athenian tilth and plains. We should either not pray at all, or else in this simple, noble sort.

editions.name: George W. Chrystal
editions.text: This is a prayer of the Athenians: “Rain, rain, dear Zeus, on the tilled fields and plains of Athens.” We ought either not to pray at all, or to pray in this simple and noble fashion.

editions.name: John Jackson
editions.text: There was a prayer of the Athenians which ran: “Rain, rain, O Zeus beloved, on the cornfields and plains of Attica.”—If we are to pray at all, let us pray like this, simply and freely.

editions.name: C. R. Haines
editions.text: A prayer of the Athenians: Rain, Rain, O dear Zeus, upon the corn-land of the Athenians, and their meads. Either pray not at all, or in this simple and frank fashion.

audit: Eleven complete English Meditations translations through 1930 were checked. James Thomson's 1747 edition omits 9.40, explaining its absence from that passage; the other passage counts reflect actual inclusion.

author: Demetrius the Cynic
title: Prayer of willing surrender
pd:
Ye immortal Gods, the only complaint which I have to make of you is that you did not make your will known to me earlier; for then I would sooner have gone into that state of life to which I now have been called. Do you wish to take my children? it was for you that I brought them up. Do you wish to take some part of my body? take it: it is no great thing that I am offering you, I shall soon have done with the whole of it.

Do you wish for my life? why should I hesitate to return to you what you gave me? whatever you ask you shall receive with my good will: nay, I would rather give it than be forced to hand it over to you: what need had you to take away what you did? you might have received it from me: yet even as it is you cannot take anything from me, because you cannot rob a man unless he resists.
source: Demetrius was a Cynic philosopher whose prayer Seneca presents approvingly in *On Providence* 5.5–6. Latin text; Stewart’s translation.
original: Di immortales, unum habeo de vobis queri, quod non ante mihi notam voluntatem vestram fecistis; prior enim ad ista venissem, ad quae nunc vocatus adsum. Vultis liberos sumere? vobis illos sustuli. Vultis aliquam partem corporis? sumite … Vultis spiritum? quidni? nullam moram faciam quo minus recipiatis quod dedistis.
accurate: Immortal gods, I have one complaint against you: that you did not make your will known to me sooner. I would have come earlier to what I have now been summoned to. Do you wish to take my children? I raised them for you. Do you wish to take some part of my body? Take it; I offer no great thing, since I shall soon relinquish the whole. Do you wish my breath of life? Why not? I shall make no delay in your receiving what you gave. Whatever you ask, I shall give willingly. What need was there to take away what you did? You could have received it from me. Even now, you cannot take anything from me, because no one is robbed unless he resists.

editions.name: Thomas Lodge
editions.text: I have heard this manly speech of Demetrius that worthy fellow: In this one thing, O immortall Gods, I can complaine of you, that you have not made knowne unto me what your will was. For to my selfe I had first of all come unto these things, to which being now called, I present my selfe. Will you take my children from me? I have brought them up to that end. Will you have a part of my body? Take it to you. I promise no great matter, I will suddenly leave all. Will you have my spirit? Why not? I will not deferre to restore that unto you, which you have bestowed upon me. I will willingly satisfie whatsoever you request. What is it then? I had rather present it you then deliver it unto you. What need had you to take away the same? You might have commanded it; neither now shall you take it away, because nothing is taken away, but that which is taken from him that detaineth the same.

editions.name: Aubrey Stewart
editions.text: Ye immortal Gods, the only complaint which I have to make of you is that you did not make your will known to me earlier; for then I would sooner have reached that condition in which, after being summoned, I now am. Do you wish to take my children? It was for you that I fathered them. Do you wish to take some part of my body? Take it: it is no great thing that I offer; I shall soon leave the whole. Do you wish to take my life? Why not? I shall not delay your taking back what you gave. Whatever you ask, you shall have with my willing consent. What, then, is my complaint? I should have preferred to offer than to surrender. What need was there to take by force? You could have received it as a gift. Even now you will not take it by force, because nothing can be torn away from a man unless he withholds it.

editions.name: J. W. Basore
editions.text: Immortal gods, I have this one complaint to make against you, that you did not earlier make known your will to me; for I should have reached the sooner that condition in which, after being summoned, I now am. Do you wish to take my children?—it was for you that I fathered them. Do you wish to take some member of my body?—take it; no great thing am I offering you; very soon I shall leave the whole. Do you wish to take my life?—why not? I shall make no protest against your taking back what once you gave. With my free consent you shall have whatever you may ask of me. What, then, is my trouble? I should have preferred to offer than to relinquish. What was the need to take by force? You might have had it as a gift. Yet even now you will not take it by force, because nothing can be wrenched away from a man unless he withholds it.

author: Aratus of Soli
title: Opening hymn and prayer in the *Phaenomena*
pd:
From Zeus let us begin; him do we mortals never leave unnamed; full of Zeus are all the streets and all the market-places of men; full is the sea and the havens thereof; always we all have need of Zeus. For we are also his offspring; and he in his kindness unto men giveth favourable signs and wakeneth the people to work, reminding them of livelihood.

He tells what time the soil is best for the labour of the ox and for the mattock, and what time the seasons are favourable both for the planting of trees and for casting all manner of seeds. For himself it was who set the signs in heaven, and marked out the constellations, and for the year devised what stars chiefly should give to men right signs of the seasons, to the end that all things might grow unfailingly. Wherefore him do men ever worship first and last.

Hail, O Father, mighty marvel, mighty blessing unto men. Hail to thee and to the Elder Race! Hail, ye Muses, right kindly, every one! But for me, too, in answer to my prayer direct all my lay, even as is meet, to tell the stars.
source: Aratus, *Phaenomena* 1–18. Aratus was associated with Zeno’s circle, but classifying him as a Stoic philosopher would be stronger than the evidence warrants. Mair’s edition and translation.
original: Ἐκ Διὸς ἀρχώμεσθα, τὸν οὐδέποτ᾽ ἄνδρες ἐῶμεν ἄρρητον· μεσταὶ δὲ Διὸς πᾶσαι μὲν ἀγυιαί, πᾶσαι δ᾽ ἀνθρώπων ἀγοραί, μεστὴ δὲ θάλασσα καὶ λιμένες· πάντη δὲ Διὸς κεχρήμεθα πάντες. τοῦ γὰρ καὶ γένος εἰμέν … χαῖρε, πάτερ, μέγα θαῦμα, μέγ᾽ ἀνθρώποισιν ὄνειαρ … αὐτὰρ ἐμοί γε εὐχομένῳ τεκμήρατε πᾶσαν ἀοιδήν.

editions.text:
Let us begin from Jove. Let every mortal raise
His grateful voice to tune Jove’s endless praise.
Jove fills the heaven—the earth—the sea—the air:
We feel his spirit moving here and every where.
And we his offspring are. He ever good
Daily provides for man his daily food.
Ordains the seasons by his signs on high,
Studding with gems of light the azure canopy.
What time with plough or spade to break the soil,
That plenteous store may bless the reaper’s toil,
What time to plant and prune the vine he shows,
And hangs the purple cluster on its boughs.
To Him—the First—the Last—all homage yield,
Our Father—Wonderful—our Help—our Shield.
Next hail, harmonious Muses, and inspire
Some portion of your own celestial fire,
Not adverse to a daring Poet’s flight,
Who scours on fancy’s wings the realms of light.

editions.name: E. Poste
editions.text:
Let us begin with Zeus, the power we mortals never leave
Unsaluted. Zeus fills all the city streets,
All the nations' crowded marts; fills the watery deeps
And havens; every labour needs the aid of Zeus.
His children are we. He benignant
Raises high signals, summoning man to toil,
And warning him of life's demands: tells when the sod is fittest
For oxen and harrows; tells the auspicious hours
For planting the sapling and casting every seed.
'Twas he who set the beacons in the sky,
And grouped the stars, and formed the annual round
Of constellations, to mark unerringly
The days when labour is crowned with increase.
Him therefore men propitiate first and last.

Hail, father, mighty marvel! hail! mighty benefactor!
Thyself and those who begot thee! And ye too, Muses,
Gracious influences, hail! and while I essay to tell of skies
What mortal may tell, guide right my wandering lay.

editions.text:
From Zeus we lead the strain, he whom mankind
Ne'er leave imhymned; of Zeus all public-ways,
All haunts of men are full, and full the sea
And harbours; and of Zeus all stand in need.
We are his offspring; and he, mild to man,
Gives favouring signs and rouses us to toil.
Calling to mind life's wants; when clods are best
For plough and mattock, when the time is ripe
For planting vines and sowing seeds he tells.
Since he himself hath fixed in heaven these signs,
The stars dividing; and throughout the year
Stars he provides to indicate to men
The seasons' course, that all things duly grow.
Him, therefore, first and last they aye appease.
Hail, Sire, vast wonder, blessing to mankind!
Hail earlier race of men! And Muses hail!
Most merciful to all; for me who hymn
The stars with reverent mind make clear the song.

author: Persius
title: The offering appropriate to prayer
pd:
O Souls bowed down to earth, and void of all heavenly thoughts! What avails it to bring our ideas into the temples, and to infer from this sinful flesh of ours what is pleasing to the gods? It is the flesh that has spoilt our oil by mingling it with casia, and misused Tyrian purple for the soaking of Calabrian fleeces; it is this that has bidden us pluck the pearl from the shell, and tear out the veins of shining ore from the native clay.

The flesh indeed sins, it sins, and yet it gets profit from its sinning. But tell me this, ye priests, what avails gold inside the sanctuary? Just as much as the dolls which maidens dedicate to Venus! Nay rather let us offer to the gods what the blear-eyed progeny of the great Messala cannot give out of his lordly salver;—a heart rightly attuned towards God and man; a mind pure in its inner depths, and a soul steeped in nobleness and honour.

Give me these to offer in the temples, and a handful of corn shall win my prayer for me!
source: Persius, *Satire* 2.61–75. Persius was a Stoic poet rather than a professional philosopher. Latin text; Ramsay’s translation.
original:
Quin damus id superis, de magna quod dare lance
non possit magni Messalae lippa propago:
compositum ius fasque animo sanctosque recessus
mentis et incoctum generoso pectus honesto.
Haec cedo ut admoveam templis, et farre litabo.
accurate: Why do we not give the gods what the bleary offspring of great Messalla could not give from a great platter: justice and divine law composed within the soul; the mind’s holy inner recesses; and a heart steeped in noble honor? Grant that I may bring these to the temples, and I shall sacrifice successfully with meal.

editions.name: John Dryden
editions.text:
But let us for the Gods a Gift prepare,
Which the Great Man's great Chargers cannot bear:
A Soul, where Laws both Humane and Divine,
In Practice more than Speculation shine:
A genuine Virtue, of a vigorous kind,
Pure in the last recesses of the Mind:
When with such Off'rings to the Gods I come;
A Cake, thus giv'n, is worth a Hecatomb.

editions.name: William Drummond
editions.text:
Let me give that, which wealth cannot bestow,
The pomp of riches, nor the glare of show;
Let me give that, which from their golden pot
Messala's proud and blear-eyed race could not:
To the just Gods let me present a mind,
Which civil and religious duties bind,
A guileless heart, which no dark secrets knows,
But with the generous love of virtue glows.
Such be the presents, such the gifts I make,
With them I sacrifice a wheaten cake.

editions.name: William Gifford
editions.text:
No; let me bring the Immortals, what the race
Of great Messala, now depraved and base,
On their huge charger, cannot;—bring a mind,
Where legal and where moral sense are join'd,
With the pure essence; holy thoughts, that dwell
In the soul's most retired, and sacred cell;
A bosom dyed in honour's noblest grain,
Deep-dyed:—with these, let me approach the fane,
And Heaven will hear the humble prayer I make,
Though all my offering be a barley cake.

editions.name: Charlton Byam Wollaston
editions.text:
Give then, what proud Messala's blear-ey'd race
Can never on their plenteous table place,
A heart where piety and justice rest,
Inwardly sound, by generous thoughts imprest.
Give me but these to offer at the shrine,
And one small cake shall sooth the pow'rs divine.

editions.name: Lewis Evans
editions.text: Why do we not offer that to the gods which the blear-eyed progeny of great Messala cannot give even from his high-heaped charger: Justice to god and man enshrined within the heart; the inner chambers of the soul free from pollution; the breast imbued with generous honour. Give me these to present at the temples, and I will make my successful offering with a little meal.

editions.name: John Conington
editions.text: Give we rather to the gods such an offering as great Messalla's blear-eyed representative has no means of giving even out of his great dish—duty to god and man well blended in the mind, purity in the shrine of the heart, and a racy flavour of nobleness pervading the bosom. Let me have these to carry to the temple, and a handful of meal shall win me acceptance.

editions.name: G. G. Ramsay
editions.text:
O Souls bowed down to earth, and void of all heavenly thoughts! What avails it to bring our ideas into the temples, and to infer from this sinful flesh of ours what is pleasing to the gods? It is the flesh that has spoilt our oil by mingling it with casia, and misused Tyrian purple for the soaking of Calabrian fleeces; it is this that has bidden us pluck the pearl from the shell, and tear out the veins of shining ore from the native clay.

The flesh indeed sins, it sins, and yet it gets profit from its sinning. But tell me this, ye priests, what avails gold inside the sanctuary? Just as much as the dolls which maidens dedicate to Venus! Nay rather let us offer to the gods what the blear-eyed progeny of the great Messala cannot give out of his lordly salver;—a heart rightly attuned towards God and man; a mind pure in its inner depths, and a soul steeped in nobleness and honour.

Give me these to offer in the temples, and a handful of corn shall win my prayer for me!

author: Euripides
title: Acceptance of necessity
pd:
Whoe’er yields properly to Fate is deemed
Wise among men, and knows the laws of Heaven.
source: Epictetus, *Enchiridion* 53. The first is a fragment of Euripides; the second adapts Plato’s *Crito*. Greek text; Higginson’s translation.
original: ὅστις δ᾽ ἀνάγκῃ συγκεχώρηκεν καλῶς, σοφὸς παρ᾽ ἡμῖν, καὶ τὰ θεῖ᾽ ἐπίσταται.
accurate: Whoever has yielded well to necessity is considered wise among us and understands divine things.

editions.name: James Sandford
editions.text: Wherefore he which willingly followeth necessity is wise.

editions.name: John Healey
editions.text: Hee that can adapt his affects unto necessity, herein performeth a part of wisdome, and is in some sorte privie to the designes of the deities.

editions.name: John Davies
editions.text:
Who can, with what's not to be shun'd comply,
Surveies the secrets of the Deity.

editions.name: Ellis Walker
editions.text:
He that submits to Destiny's decrees,
Is justly counted wise by Men, and knows
The due respects, which to the Gods he owes.

editions.name: J. W.
editions.text:
Who treats Necessity with due Regard,
Is wise, and understands the heavenly Word.

editions.name: William Bond (“a Person of Quality”)
editions.text: To comply with the necessity of the times, and yet retain an untainted innocence, evinces a profound wisdom.

editions.name: Elizabeth Carter
editions.text:
Whoever yields properly to Fate, is deemed
Wise among men, and knows the laws of heaven.

editions.name: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu
editions.text: He is a wise man, who submits himself to necessity, and is conscious of the Divine Providence.

editions.name: Henry McCormac
editions.text: But he who yields a cheerful assent is justly reckoned wise; his knowledge is indeed divine.

editions.name: Thomas Talbot
editions.text:
Who walks unmoved thro' life's e'er-changing state,
And cheerful yields to the decrees of Fate,
May scorn those ills which weaker minds o'erpower,
And win sweet regards from those in Heaven above.

editions.name: George Long
editions.text:
But whoso nobly yields unto necessity,
We hold him wise, and skill’d in things divine.

editions.name: T. W. H. Rolleston
editions.text: That man is wise among us, and has understanding of things divine, who has nobly agreed with Necessity.

editions.name: Thomas Wentworth Higginson
editions.text:
Whoe’er yields properly to Fate is deemed
Wise among men, and knows the laws of Heaven.

editions.name: P. E. Matheson
editions.text:
Who rightly with necessity complies
In things divine we count him skilled and wise.

editions.name: W. A. Oldfather
editions.text:
Whoso has rightly with necessity complied,
We count him wise, and skilled in things divine.

author: Socrates
title: Acceptance of the gods’ will
pd: O Crito, if it thus pleases the gods, thus let it be.
source: Epictetus, *Enchiridion* 53. The first is a fragment of Euripides; the second adapts Plato’s *Crito*. Greek text; Higginson’s translation.
original: ἀλλ᾽, ὦ Κρίτων, εἰ ταύτῃ τοῖς θεοῖς φίλον, ταύτῃ γενέσθω.
accurate: But, Crito, if this way is pleasing to the gods, let it happen this way.

editions.name: James Sandford
editions.text: O Crito, if it so please God, so be it. Anitus truly and Melitus may well kill me, but to hurt me, it lieth not in their power.

editions.name: John Healey
editions.text: Why if it bee GODS pleasure, Crito, GODS pleasure be fullfilled: It is in the power of Anytus and Melitus to kill mee, but to doe mee any hurt, is a thing surmounting all their proiects whatso-ever.

editions.name: John Davies
editions.text:
If the Great Gods, dear Friend, have minuted
The dreadful Tempest which hangs ore my head,
If, of my Death, the dire Decree be sign'd,
I acquiesce, with a submissive mind.
I, of my Life, would not prolong the date,
Beyond the stinted limits of my Fate:
Of my few dayes my Enemies dispose,
'Tis in their Power their hasty course to close:
To that my Body, mortal, needs must bend,
But still my mind their malice does transcend:
And though I, to their Rage, a Victim fall,
My Faith and Virtue know no Funeral.

editions.name: Ellis Walker
editions.text:
O Crito, if it please the Gods, that I,
To please the rage of Enemies, must die,
Let it be so, the false Anytus may,
With false Melitus, take my Life away,
But cannot hurt me, or my Soul dismay.

editions.name: J. W.
editions.text:
If this Decree from Destiny doth run,
Dear Crito, let the Will of Heaven be done.
Anytus and Melitus may destroy
This mortal Body, but can't hurt my Joy.

editions.name: William Bond (“a Person of Quality”)
editions.text: Submit yourself to the disposition of the gods. Anitus and Melitus have a power over this body to kill it, when they please; but cannot injure my nobler part.

editions.name: Elizabeth Carter
editions.text: O Crito, if it thus pleases the gods, thus let it be. Anytus and Melitus may kill me indeed, but hurt me they cannot.

editions.name: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu
editions.text: And this, O Crito, is the wisest prayer, if so it seems best to the gods, so be it. Anytus and Melitus have the power to kill me, but they have not the power to hurt me.

editions.name: Henry McCormac
editions.text: Crito, if it please God, let it be so; Anytus and Melitus may take away my life, but they cannot injure my soul!

editions.name: George Long
editions.text: O Crito, if so it pleases the Gods, so let it be; Anytus and Melitus are able indeed to kill me, but they cannot harm me.

editions.name: T. W. H. Rolleston
editions.text: O Crito, if so it seem good to the Gods, so let it be; Anytus and Melitus are able to kill me if they like, but to harm me, never.

editions.name: Thomas Wentworth Higginson
editions.text: O Crito, if it thus pleases the gods, thus let it be. Anytus and Melitus may kill me indeed; but hurt me they cannot.

editions.name: P. E. Matheson
editions.text: Well, Crito, if this be the gods’ will, so be it. Anytus and Meletus have power to put me to death, but not to harm me.

editions.name: W. A. Oldfather
editions.text: Well, O Crito, if so it is pleasing to the gods, so let it be. Anytus and Meletus can kill me, but they cannot hurt me.
